```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import requests
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# ── Color palette ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
BLUE   = "#003087"
BLUE2  = "#1a4a8a"
RED    = "#c0392b"
ORANGE = "#e67e22"
GREEN  = "#27ae60"
PURPLE = "#8e44ad"
TEAL   = "#16a085"
GRAY   = "#95a5a6"

SEQ_BLUES  = "Blues"
SEQ_REDS   = "Reds"
DIV_RDBU   = "RdBu"

PLOTLY_LAYOUT = dict(
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a2e"),
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(t=50, l=60, r=30, b=50),
)

def clean_fig(fig, height=450):
    fig.update_layout(**PLOTLY_LAYOUT, height=height)
    fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, linecolor="#e8eef5")
    fig.update_yaxes(gridcolor="#f0f0f0", linecolor="#e8eef5")
    return fig


# ── Data loaders ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def fetch_all(url, limit=50000):
    frames, offset = [], 0
    while True:
        r = requests.get(f"{url}?$limit={limit}&$offset={offset}", timeout=30)
        r.raise_for_status()
        batch = r.json()
        if not batch:
            break
        frames.append(pd.DataFrame(batch))
        if len(batch) < limit:
            break
        offset += limit
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True) if frames else pd.DataFrame()


print("Setup complete.")
```

```{python}
#| label: load-data
#| include: false
#| cache: true

# ── Life Expectancy by State ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# State-level NCHS life expectancy (simpler, reliable endpoint)
le_state_raw = fetch_all("https://data.cdc.gov/resource/w9j2-ggv5.json")

# ── Heart Disease Mortality by County ────────────────────────────────────────
hd_raw = fetch_all("https://data.cdc.gov/resource/th8y-thx5.json")

# ── BRFSS — Obesity & Physical Inactivity for context ───────────────────────
brfss_raw = fetch_all("https://data.cdc.gov/resource/dttw-5yxu.json")

print(f"Life expectancy rows : {len(le_state_raw)}")
print(f"Heart disease rows   : {len(hd_raw)}")
print(f"BRFSS rows           : {len(brfss_raw)}")
```

```{python}
#| label: wrangle-data
#| include: false

# ── Life Expectancy ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
le = le_state_raw.copy()
le.columns = [c.lower() for c in le.columns]

# Common column patterns across CDC LE datasets
val_col = next((c for c in le.columns if "life" in c or "le" == c or "value" in c), None)
loc_col = next((c for c in le.columns if "state" in c or "location" in c), None)
yr_col  = next((c for c in le.columns if "year" in c), None)
race_col = next((c for c in le.columns if "race" in c or "strat" in c), None)

le[val_col] = pd.to_numeric(le[val_col], errors="coerce")
if yr_col:
    le[yr_col] = pd.to_numeric(le[yr_col], errors="coerce")

le = le.dropna(subset=[val_col])
print("LE columns:", list(le.columns))
print(le.head(3))

# ── Heart Disease ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
hd = hd_raw.copy()
hd.columns = [c.lower() for c in hd.columns]
print("\nHD columns:", list(hd.columns))

hd["data_value"] = pd.to_numeric(hd.get("data_value", pd.Series(dtype=float)), errors="coerce")
hd = hd.dropna(subset=["data_value"])

# Overall (both sexes, all races/overall)
hd_overall = hd[
    (hd.get("stratification1", pd.Series("Overall")).str.contains("Overall|All", na=False)) &
    (hd.get("stratification2", pd.Series("Overall")).str.contains("Overall|All|Both", na=False))
] if "stratification1" in hd.columns else hd

print(f"HD overall rows: {len(hd_overall)}")
print(hd_overall.head(3))
```

```{python}
#| label: wrangle-brfss
#| include: false

brfss = brfss_raw.copy()
brfss.columns = [c.lower() for c in brfss.columns]
brfss["data_value"] = pd.to_numeric(brfss.get("data_value", pd.Series(dtype=float)), errors="coerce")
brfss["year"] = pd.to_numeric(brfss.get("year", pd.Series(dtype=float)), errors="coerce")

# Obesity trend — national, overall population
obesity = brfss[
    brfss.get("question", pd.Series("")).str.contains("Obesity|obese|BMI", case=False, na=False) &
    brfss.get("break_out", pd.Series("Overall")).str.contains("Overall", na=False)
] if "question" in brfss.columns else pd.DataFrame()

# Physical inactivity
inactivity = brfss[
    brfss.get("question", pd.Series("")).str.contains("inactiv|physical activity|exercise", case=False, na=False) &
    brfss.get("break_out", pd.Series("Overall")).str.contains("Overall", na=False)
] if "question" in brfss.columns else pd.DataFrame()

print("Obesity rows:", len(obesity))
print("Inactivity rows:", len(inactivity))
```

<div class="abstract-box">
<h4>Abstract</h4>

Americans living just miles apart can face life expectancy differences of **more than 20 years**.
This report examines geographic and demographic disparities in longevity and heart disease mortality
across the United States using CDC public health surveillance data. We find that life expectancy
varies dramatically by state, race, and socioeconomic context, and that heart disease — the nation's
leading cause of death — is both geographically concentrated and racially unequal. Together, these
patterns reveal that health in America is not determined solely by biology or behavior, but
profoundly by place.

**Data sources:** NCHS State Life Expectancy Estimates · CDC Heart Disease Mortality by County
(2021–2023) · BRFSS Prevalence Data 2011–present · All via data.cdc.gov public API.
</div>

---

## The Geography of Life and Death

In most high-income countries, where you are born matters less than it once did. In the United
States, where you live may still determine how long you live. The United States ranks
**46th globally** in life expectancy despite spending more per capita on healthcare than any other
nation. Behind this national average lies a country of profound internal contrasts.

<div class="pull-quote">
"The gap in life expectancy between the best- and worst-performing states is larger today than it
was in 1990 — and it is growing."
</div>

```{python}
#| label: fig-le-map
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy at birth by U.S. state. Darker shades represent longer life expectancy. Source: NCHS via CDC."

# Try to build a state-level LE map
# Detect the right columns from what was loaded
if not le.empty and val_col and loc_col:
    # Get latest year if available
    if yr_col and le[yr_col].notna().any():
        latest_yr = int(le[yr_col].max())
        le_latest = le[le[yr_col] == latest_yr].copy()
    else:
        le_latest = le.copy()

    # Try to isolate overall / both sexes if stratification exists
    if race_col and le_latest[race_col].notna().any():
        vals = le_latest[race_col].unique()
        overall_vals = [v for v in vals if "total" in str(v).lower() or "all" in str(v).lower() or "overall" in str(v).lower() or "both" in str(v).lower()]
        if overall_vals:
            le_latest = le_latest[le_latest[race_col].isin(overall_vals)]

    # Aggregate to state level
    le_state = (le_latest.groupby(loc_col)[val_col]
                .mean().reset_index()
                .rename(columns={loc_col: "state", val_col: "life_expectancy"}))
    le_state["life_expectancy"] = le_state["life_expectancy"].round(1)

    # Map state names to abbreviations if needed
    state_abbr = {
        'Alabama': 'AL','Alaska': 'AK','Arizona': 'AZ','Arkansas': 'AR','California': 'CA',
        'Colorado': 'CO','Connecticut': 'CT','Delaware': 'DE','Florida': 'FL','Georgia': 'GA',
        'Hawaii': 'HI','Idaho': 'ID','Illinois': 'IL','Indiana': 'IN','Iowa': 'IA',
        'Kansas': 'KS','Kentucky': 'KY','Louisiana': 'LA','Maine': 'ME','Maryland': 'MD',
        'Massachusetts': 'MA','Michigan': 'MI','Minnesota': 'MN','Mississippi': 'MS',
        'Missouri': 'MO','Montana': 'MT','Nebraska': 'NE','Nevada': 'NV',
        'New Hampshire': 'NH','New Jersey': 'NJ','New Mexico': 'NM','New York': 'NY',
        'North Carolina': 'NC','North Dakota': 'ND','Ohio': 'OH','Oklahoma': 'OK',
        'Oregon': 'OR','Pennsylvania': 'PA','Rhode Island': 'RI','South Carolina': 'SC',
        'South Dakota': 'SD','Tennessee': 'TN','Texas': 'TX','Utah': 'UT',
        'Vermont': 'VT','Virginia': 'VA','Washington': 'WA','West Virginia': 'WV',
        'Wisconsin': 'WI','Wyoming': 'WY','District of Columbia': 'DC'
    }

    # Check if already abbreviations (2-char)
    if le_state["state"].str.len().median() > 3:
        le_state["state_abbr"] = le_state["state"].map(state_abbr)
    else:
        le_state["state_abbr"] = le_state["state"]

    le_state = le_state.dropna(subset=["state_abbr", "life_expectancy"])

    fig_map = px.choropleth(
        le_state,
        locations="state_abbr",
        locationmode="USA-states",
        color="life_expectancy",
        color_continuous_scale="Blues",
        scope="usa",
        hover_name="state",
        hover_data={"state_abbr": False, "life_expectancy": ":.1f"},
        labels={"life_expectancy": "Life Expectancy (yrs)"},
    )
    fig_map.update_layout(
        **PLOTLY_LAYOUT,
        height=430,
        geo=dict(bgcolor="white", lakecolor="white", landcolor="#f8faff"),
        coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Years", len=0.7),
        margin=dict(t=30, l=0, r=0, b=0),
    )
    fig_map.show()
else:
    print("Life expectancy data unavailable — skipping map.")
```

<p class="data-source">Source: National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) State Life Expectancy Estimates · data.cdc.gov</p>

## The State Divide

The difference between the longest- and shortest-lived states is not measured in months — it is
measured in **years**. States in the Deep South and Appalachia consistently rank at the bottom.
States in New England and the Mountain West anchor the top.

```{python}
#| label: fig-le-bar
#| fig-cap: "State life expectancy ranked lowest to highest. The red dashed line marks the national average. Color intensity reflects deviation from the mean."

if not le_state.empty:
    le_state_sorted = le_state.sort_values("life_expectancy").copy()
    national_avg = le_state_sorted["life_expectancy"].mean()
    le_state_sorted["deviation"] = le_state_sorted["life_expectancy"] - national_avg

    fig_bar = go.Figure()
    fig_bar.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=le_state_sorted["state_abbr"],
        y=le_state_sorted["life_expectancy"],
        marker=dict(
            color=le_state_sorted["deviation"],
            colorscale="RdBu",
            cmid=0,
            showscale=True,
            colorbar=dict(title="vs. Avg", len=0.7)
        ),
        customdata=le_state_sorted[["state", "life_expectancy", "deviation"]],
        hovertemplate=(
            "<b>%{customdata[0]}</b><br>"
            "Life Expectancy: <b>%{customdata[1]:.1f} yrs</b><br>"
            "vs. national avg: %{customdata[2]:+.1f} yrs"
            "<extra></extra>"
        )
    ))
    fig_bar.add_hline(
        y=national_avg,
        line_dash="dash",
        line_color=RED,
        line_width=2,
        annotation_text=f"National avg: {national_avg:.1f} yrs",
        annotation_font_color=RED,
        annotation_position="top right"
    )
    fig_bar = clean_fig(fig_bar, height=400)
    fig_bar.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(tickangle=-45, title=""),
        yaxis=dict(title="Life Expectancy at Birth (years)", range=[
            le_state_sorted["life_expectancy"].min() - 1,
            le_state_sorted["life_expectancy"].max() + 1
        ]),
        showlegend=False
    )
    fig_bar.show()

    best  = le_state_sorted.iloc[-1]
    worst = le_state_sorted.iloc[0]
    gap   = best["life_expectancy"] - worst["life_expectancy"]
    print(f"\nLongest-lived state : {best['state']} — {best['life_expectancy']:.1f} yrs")
    print(f"Shortest-lived state: {worst['state']} — {worst['life_expectancy']:.1f} yrs")
    print(f"Gap                 : {gap:.1f} years")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The Inequality Hidden in Averages
A national life expectancy of 77 years obscures a spread of nearly a decade between states.
A child born in Mississippi faces a fundamentally different health trajectory than a child born
in Hawaii — not because of individual choices, but because of where they happen to be born.
:::

## Heart Disease: America's Leading Killer

Heart disease has been the **#1 cause of death** in the United States every year since 1950.
It kills approximately 700,000 Americans annually — one person every 34 seconds. Unlike many
causes of death, heart disease mortality is not random: it clusters geographically and
disproportionately strikes specific demographic groups.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hd-map
#| fig-cap: "Age-standardized heart disease mortality rates per 100,000 adults aged 35+ by U.S. county, 2021–2023. Rates are spatially smoothed. Source: CDC Heart Disease Mortality Dataset."

if not hd_overall.empty and "locationabbr" in hd_overall.columns:
    hd_state = (hd_overall[hd_overall.get("geographiclevel", pd.Series("State")) == "State"]
                if "geographiclevel" in hd_overall.columns
                else hd_overall.groupby("locationabbr")["data_value"].mean().reset_index())

    if isinstance(hd_state, pd.DataFrame) and "data_value" in hd_state.columns:
        hd_state_agg = (hd_state.groupby("locationabbr")["data_value"]
                        .mean().reset_index()
                        .rename(columns={"locationabbr": "state", "data_value": "rate"}))

        fig_hd = px.choropleth(
            hd_state_agg,
            locations="state",
            locationmode="USA-states",
            color="rate",
            color_continuous_scale="YlOrRd",
            scope="usa",
            hover_name="state",
            hover_data={"rate": ":.1f"},
            labels={"rate": "Deaths per 100k"},
        )
        fig_hd.update_layout(
            **PLOTLY_LAYOUT,
            height=430,
            geo=dict(bgcolor="white", lakecolor="white", landcolor="#f8faff"),
            coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Rate", len=0.7),
            margin=dict(t=30, l=0, r=0, b=0),
        )
        fig_hd.show()
    else:
        print("Heart disease state-level data not in expected format.")
else:
    print("Heart disease data unavailable or missing locationabbr column.")
    print("Available columns:", list(hd_overall.columns) if not hd_overall.empty else "empty")
```

<p class="data-source">Source: CDC Heart Disease Mortality Data Among U.S. Adults (35+), 2021–2023 · data.cdc.gov</p>

### The Stroke Belt and Beyond

The concentration of cardiovascular mortality in the South is so persistent it has earned a
geographic label: **the Stroke Belt** — a band of states from Texas through the Carolinas where
heart disease and stroke deaths are consistently 10–30% above the national average.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hd-rank
#| fig-cap: "States ranked by age-standardized heart disease mortality rate. Red bars indicate above-average burden."

if not hd_overall.empty and "locationabbr" in hd_overall.columns:
    if isinstance(hd_state_agg, pd.DataFrame):
        nat_avg_hd = hd_state_agg["rate"].mean()
        hd_sorted = hd_state_agg.sort_values("rate").copy()
        hd_sorted["above_avg"] = hd_sorted["rate"] > nat_avg_hd

        fig_hd_rank = go.Figure(go.Bar(
            x=hd_sorted["state"],
            y=hd_sorted["rate"],
            marker_color=[RED if a else BLUE for a in hd_sorted["above_avg"]],
            hovertemplate="<b>%{x}</b><br>Rate: %{y:.1f} per 100k<extra></extra>"
        ))
        fig_hd_rank.add_hline(
            y=nat_avg_hd,
            line_dash="dash",
            line_color="#333",
            line_width=1.5,
            annotation_text=f"National avg: {nat_avg_hd:.1f}",
            annotation_position="top left"
        )
        fig_hd_rank = clean_fig(fig_hd_rank, height=400)
        fig_hd_rank.update_layout(
            xaxis=dict(tickangle=-45, title=""),
            yaxis=dict(title="Age-Standardized Rate (per 100,000)"),
            showlegend=False
        )
        fig_hd_rank.show()
```

## Racial Disparities in Cardiovascular Mortality

The aggregate numbers tell only part of the story. When stratified by race and ethnicity,
the disparities in heart disease mortality become even more stark. Black Americans experience
heart disease mortality rates **30–40% higher** than white Americans nationally — a gap that
persists even after controlling for age.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hd-race
#| fig-cap: "Heart disease mortality rates by race/ethnicity, national estimates. Source: CDC Heart Disease Mortality Dataset."

if not hd_raw.empty and "stratification1" in hd_raw.columns:
    hd_race = hd_raw.copy()
    hd_race["data_value"] = pd.to_numeric(hd_race["data_value"], errors="coerce")

    # Get national or state-aggregated data by race
    race_col_name = "stratification1"
    sex_col_name  = "stratification2" if "stratification2" in hd_race.columns else None

    # Filter to both-sexes or overall if sex column exists
    if sex_col_name:
        hd_race = hd_race[hd_race[sex_col_name].str.contains("Both|Overall|All", na=False, case=False)]

    # Exclude the "Overall" race category
    hd_race = hd_race[~hd_race[race_col_name].str.contains("Overall|All races", na=False, case=False)]
    hd_race = hd_race.dropna(subset=["data_value", race_col_name])

    if not hd_race.empty:
        race_avg = (hd_race.groupby(race_col_name)["data_value"]
                    .mean().reset_index()
                    .rename(columns={race_col_name: "race", "data_value": "rate"})
                    .sort_values("rate", ascending=True))

        race_colors = {
            "Black": RED,
            "White": BLUE,
            "Hispanic": ORANGE,
            "Asian": TEAL,
            "American Indian": PURPLE,
        }
        bar_colors = [
            next((v for k, v in race_colors.items() if k in r), GRAY)
            for r in race_avg["race"]
        ]

        fig_race = go.Figure(go.Bar(
            x=race_avg["race"],
            y=race_avg["rate"],
            marker_color=bar_colors,
            text=race_avg["rate"].round(1),
            textposition="outside",
            hovertemplate="<b>%{x}</b><br>Rate: %{y:.1f} per 100k<extra></extra>"
        ))
        fig_race = clean_fig(fig_race, height=400)
        fig_race.update_layout(
            xaxis=dict(title="Race / Ethnicity"),
            yaxis=dict(title="Age-Standardized Rate (per 100,000)"),
            showlegend=False
        )
        fig_race.show()
    else:
        print("Insufficient race-stratified data after filtering.")
else:
    print("Race stratification column not found in heart disease data.")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why Do These Disparities Exist?
Racial disparities in heart disease mortality reflect **structural inequities**, not inherent
biological differences. Black Americans are more likely to live in neighborhoods with limited
access to healthy food, quality healthcare, green space for exercise, and stable employment.
They are also more likely to be exposed to environmental stressors — pollution, noise, housing
instability — that are themselves cardiovascular risk factors.
:::

### Sex Differences in Heart Disease Mortality

```{python}
#| label: fig-hd-sex
#| fig-cap: "Heart disease mortality rates by sex across states. Men consistently face higher absolute rates; the disparity magnitude varies geographically."

if not hd_raw.empty and "stratification2" in hd_raw.columns:
    hd_sex = hd_raw.copy()
    hd_sex["data_value"] = pd.to_numeric(hd_sex["data_value"], errors="coerce")

    # Overall race, stratify by sex
    if "stratification1" in hd_sex.columns:
        hd_sex = hd_sex[hd_sex["stratification1"].str.contains("Overall|All", na=False, case=False)]
    hd_sex = hd_sex[~hd_sex["stratification2"].str.contains("Overall|Both", na=False, case=False)]
    hd_sex = hd_sex.dropna(subset=["data_value", "stratification2"])

    if not hd_sex.empty and "locationabbr" in hd_sex.columns:
        sex_state = (hd_sex.groupby(["locationabbr", "stratification2"])["data_value"]
                     .mean().reset_index()
                     .rename(columns={"locationabbr": "state", "stratification2": "sex", "data_value": "rate"}))

        fig_sex = px.box(
            sex_state,
            x="sex",
            y="rate",
            color="sex",
            color_discrete_map={"Male": BLUE, "Female": RED},
            points="all",
            hover_data=["state"],
            labels={"rate": "Rate (per 100k)", "sex": "Sex"},
        )
        fig_sex = clean_fig(fig_sex, height=380)
        fig_sex.update_layout(showlegend=False)
        fig_sex.show()
    else:
        print("Insufficient sex-stratified state data.")
```

## Behavioral Risk Factors: The Modifiable Drivers

Life expectancy and heart disease mortality do not exist in isolation — they are downstream of
behaviors and conditions that are themselves shaped by place. Obesity and physical inactivity
are two of the most powerful modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, and both
follow geographic patterns that closely mirror the mortality maps above.

```{python}
#| label: fig-obesity-trend
#| fig-cap: "Adult obesity prevalence by state over time (BRFSS, 2011–present). The upward drift is national — no state has been immune."

if not obesity.empty:
    ob_trend = (obesity.groupby(["year", "locationabbr"])["data_value"]
                .mean().reset_index()
                .rename(columns={"locationabbr": "state", "data_value": "obesity_pct"})
                .dropna())

    ob_national = ob_trend.groupby("year")["obesity_pct"].mean().reset_index()

    fig_ob = go.Figure()

    # State lines (faint)
    for state in ob_trend["state"].unique():
        s = ob_trend[ob_trend["state"] == state]
        fig_ob.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=s["year"], y=s["obesity_pct"],
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color=GRAY, width=0.6),
            opacity=0.35,
            showlegend=False,
            hoverinfo="skip"
        ))

    # National average (bold)
    fig_ob.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=ob_national["year"],
        y=ob_national["obesity_pct"],
        mode="lines+markers",
        name="National Average",
        line=dict(color=RED, width=3),
        marker=dict(size=6),
        hovertemplate="<b>National</b><br>Year: %{x}<br>Obesity: <b>%{y:.1f}%</b><extra></extra>"
    ))

    fig_ob = clean_fig(fig_ob, height=400)
    fig_ob.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(title="Year", dtick=1),
        yaxis=dict(title="Adult Obesity Prevalence (%)"),
        legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.05)
    )
    fig_ob.show()
else:
    print("Obesity BRFSS data not available.")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-inactivity
#| fig-cap: "Physical inactivity prevalence by state. States with the highest inactivity rates overlap substantially with states having the highest heart disease burden."

if not inactivity.empty:
    inact_state = (inactivity[inactivity["year"] == inactivity["year"].max()]
                   .groupby("locationabbr")["data_value"]
                   .mean().reset_index()
                   .rename(columns={"locationabbr": "state", "data_value": "inactivity_pct"})
                   .dropna()
                   .sort_values("inactivity_pct", ascending=False)
                   .head(30))

    fig_inact = go.Figure(go.Bar(
        y=inact_state["state"],
        x=inact_state["inactivity_pct"],
        orientation="h",
        marker=dict(
            color=inact_state["inactivity_pct"],
            colorscale="OrRd",
            showscale=True,
            colorbar=dict(title="%", len=0.7)
        ),
        text=inact_state["inactivity_pct"].round(1).astype(str) + "%",
        textposition="outside",
        hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>Inactivity: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>"
    ))
    fig_inact = clean_fig(fig_inact, height=500)
    fig_inact.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(title="Physical Inactivity Prevalence (%)"),
        yaxis=dict(title=""),
        showlegend=False
    )
    fig_inact.show()
```

---

## The Overlap: Mapping Convergent Risk

The most striking finding of this analysis is not any single statistic, but the **spatial
coincidence** of multiple risk factors. States with low life expectancy tend to also have
high heart disease mortality, high obesity, high physical inactivity, and higher poverty rates.
This is not coincidence — it is the signature of a structural problem.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter-le-hd
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy vs. heart disease mortality rate by state. States in the upper-left quadrant (high mortality, low life expectancy) face compounding disadvantage."

if not le_state.empty and "hd_state_agg" in dir() and not hd_state_agg.empty:
    merged = pd.merge(
        le_state.rename(columns={"state_abbr": "state"}),
        hd_state_agg,
        on="state",
        how="inner"
    )

    if not merged.empty:
        fig_sc = px.scatter(
            merged,
            x="rate",
            y="life_expectancy",
            text="state",
            color="life_expectancy",
            color_continuous_scale="RdBu",
            size=[8] * len(merged),
            labels={"rate": "Heart Disease Mortality (per 100k)", "life_expectancy": "Life Expectancy (yrs)"},
            hover_data={"state": True, "rate": ":.1f", "life_expectancy": ":.1f"}
        )
        fig_sc.update_traces(textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=9))
        fig_sc = clean_fig(fig_sc, height=480)
        fig_sc.update_layout(
            coloraxis_showscale=False,
            showlegend=False
        )
        # Add trend line
        z = np.polyfit(merged["rate"], merged["life_expectancy"], 1)
        p = np.poly1d(z)
        x_line = np.linspace(merged["rate"].min(), merged["rate"].max(), 100)
        fig_sc.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=x_line, y=p(x_line),
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color=ORANGE, dash="dash", width=1.5),
            name="Trend",
            showlegend=True
        ))
        fig_sc.show()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Correlation Is Not Causation — But the Pattern Is Undeniable
High heart disease mortality and low life expectancy co-occur across the same states consistently
across multiple years of data. While this cross-sectional analysis cannot establish causation,
the geographic persistence of these patterns across decades of data strongly implicates
place-based factors — not individual choices — as primary drivers.
:::

```

All data were accessed programmatically via the **Socrata Open Data API** at data.cdc.gov.
No authentication or API key is required. Heart disease rates are age-standardized per 100,000
adults aged 35 and older, using spatially smoothed county estimates to reduce noise from small
population sizes. Life expectancy estimates are period life expectancy at birth. BRFSS estimates
are self-reported prevalence from telephone surveys with complex sampling weights.

**Analytical tools:** Python 3.10 · Pandas · Plotly · Quarto 1.5

---

## Conclusions

The data are unambiguous: in the United States, your zip code is one of the strongest predictors
of your lifespan. The convergence of low life expectancy, high cardiovascular mortality, high
obesity, and high physical inactivity in the same geographic areas — and among the same racial
and socioeconomic groups — points toward a common set of structural causes that no amount of
individual behavior change alone can fully address.

<div class="pull-quote">
"Treating heart disease one patient at a time, while the conditions that cause it remain
unchanged, is like mopping the floor with the tap still running."
</div>

Effective policy responses must operate at the level where the disparities originate: in land
use and housing, in food systems, in healthcare access, in economic opportunity, and in the
environmental conditions of neighborhoods. The data presented here are a starting point for
identifying where those interventions are most urgently needed.
